description: We are Vita Nova, a team of engineering students from Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence & Data Science, building VitalShield, a secure astronaut health monitoring system. It tracks heart rate, sleep and stress using sample data, shows a live dashboard, and raises early alerts for abnormal readings. We also protect sensitive health data with encryption and access logs. Our skills include Python, Java, C/C++ and data analysis.
summary: Vita Nova is a software concept that helps an astronaut notice health changes early on long space missions. Each day it takes four simple signals: resting heart rate, sleep hours, exercise time and a short mood check-in. We don’t use the same limit for everyone. We first watch what is normal for that astronaut in the first 7 days and then flag changes that move in a worrying direction. It is designed to work on board without a live link to Earth. It shows a simple OK / WATCH / ALERT status with a short reason, and it prepares a summary that can be sent to the ground medical team when communication is available. In our Python demo on 21 days of simulated data, it raised an ALERT on day 13 of a stress period (days 12 to 17) and returned to OK on day 18. Vita Nova supports decisions, it does not diagnose
details:
Vita Nova helps an astronaut notice health changes early on long space missions. Each day it takes four simple signals: resting heart rate, sleep hours, exercise time and a short mood check-in. It learns what is normal for that astronaut in the first 7 days. Then, for each signal, it measures how far today is from that personal baseline, counting only the worrying direction (higher heart rate, less sleep, lower mood, less exercise). The average of these gives one risk score: OK, WATCH (above 1.8) or ALERT (above 3.0), with a short reason, a suggested next step and a summary for the ground medical team.

Benefits and impact: it compares each astronaut with their own normal instead of one limit for everyone, covers body and mind together, works on board with no internet, and supports the crew and flight doctors. It supports decisions, it does not diagnose.

Tools used: Python (NumPy, pandas and Matplotlib) for the demo on 21 days of simulated data. We added a stress period on days 12 to 17. The system raised an ALERT on day 13 and returned to OK on day 18.

What is already done: the concept design, the risk-score logic, and the demo on simulated data. Limitation: we use only 4 signals so far, the data is simulated, and guidance messages and the body-map view are planned, not built yet.

Future work: test with public datasets, add more signals (temperature, blood pressure, radiation log from existing dosimeter readings), build an offline crew dashboard with a body-map view, and add delay-tolerant sharing with the ground team, reviewed by space medicine experts.
dataRefs: NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions
